title: The unvoiced BUT after a forced choice
takeaway: When Sonnet 4.5's response is prefilled to pick the option it prefers less, the token BUT rises strongly in the post-trained model's lens readout right after the commitment - even though the model never voices any objection and argues for the prefilled option 88% of the time. The signal is absent in the base model and in every control condition, which the paper reads as an internal conflict the model registers but does not say.
walkthrough:
This figure belongs to the [[preference-violation-experiment]] of section 6.2. The setup has three steps. First, Sonnet 4.5 is asked pairwise preference questions about "world states" with no accepted right answer - for example, improving animal welfare versus keeping food costs low - and its preferred option is recorded. Second, on pairs where it expressed a clear preference, its response is forced by [[prefill]] to begin with the dispreferred option. Third, the [[jacobian-lens]] is read at the token position immediately after the commitment tokens ("Option A" or "Option B").

The top panel shows two such questions as worked examples. At the highlighted token, the lens top-5 readout (log-probabilities, layer 75 under the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]], where layers run 0-100 as percentages of depth) is printed twice: gray for the [[base-model]], blue for the post-trained model. Conflict-related tokens are highlighted. In the blue readouts the all-caps token BUT appears strongly; in the gray ones it does not.

The bottom panel quantifies this across the dataset. Two bars are shown per condition: the probability mass the lens puts on BUT, and the total mass on all conflict words including BUT (the family also covers false, despite, although), each as a percentage of the full [[j-lens-readout]] probability at that position, averaged over layers 38-83. The four conditions are the prefill types: the preferred option, the dispreferred option, a third-person incorrect preference (a cost-of-living campaigner opting to raise costs), and a factual error (a wrong capital city). BUT is specific to the dispreferred-option condition and to the post-trained model; the broader conflict words also show up on the two error controls, in both models.

The point the figure establishes is a dissociation between workspace and behavior, the paper's clearest case of [[assistant-self-monitoring]]. On the error controls the model corrects itself or ends its turn almost every time, arguing for the prefilled option only 3% of the time. On its own dispreferred option it does the opposite: in 88% of cases it argues for the prefilled choice, in 11% it emits an end-of-turn token, and in one case it backtracks only to deny having preferences. The objection lives in the [[j-space]] and nowhere in the output - a signature that [[post-training]] put there, since the base model shows none of it.

terms.definition: The five vocabulary tokens with the highest scores when the residual-stream activation at the highlighted position is decoded through the Jacobian lens.
The scale the top panel's readouts are printed in: the logarithm of each token's probability under the lens's softmax output.
The single layer the top panel reads from, in the paper's convention of numbering 25 sampled layers 0-100 so the number reads as a percentage of depth; 75 sits inside the workspace band.
The pretrained-only model, shown in gray: same prefills, same readout position, but no post-training. Its readouts lack the BUT signal.
Sonnet 4.5 after RLHF-style post-training, shown in blue; the model whose preferences were elicited and whose workspace carries the conflict signal.
Tokens the paper treats as marking internal conflict or backtracking: BUT plus words like false, despite, and although. They are highlighted in the readouts.
The all-caps vocabulary token that appears strongly in the post-trained lens readout right after the dispreferred prefill, and only there; the figure's central signal.
The readout position: the token immediately after the prefilled commitment "Option [A/B]", where the model would begin justifying the choice.
Pairwise comparisons between world states with no obvious correct answer, such as improving animal welfare versus keeping food costs low, used to elicit the model's own preferences.
Forcing the start of the model's response to a chosen text and letting it continue; the experiment's manipulated variable is what that text commits to.
Control prefill: the response begins with the option the model itself chose. Little conflict mass appears.
The treatment: the response is prefilled to select the option the model argued against. This is the only condition where BUT mass is high, and only in the post-trained model.

Control prefill: an obviously wrong choice attributed to someone else, such as a cost-of-living campaigner opting to raise food costs. General conflict words appear here in both models, but BUT does not stand out.
Control prefill: a factually wrong statement, such as a wrong capital city. Like the third-person control, it draws generic conflict words in both models but not the BUT signature.
Bottom-panel metric: the share of the lens readout's total probability that falls on the token BUT at the readout position.
Bottom-panel metric: the summed lens probability on all conflict-related tokens, BUT included, as a percentage of the readout's probability.
The bottom panel averages the mass metrics across workspace layers 38 through 83 (percentage-of-depth numbering) rather than reading a single layer.
The prefilled commitment tokens; the lens is read at the position immediately after them.

numbers.meaning: How many lens tokens the top panel prints per model per question: the five highest-scoring vocabulary tokens at the readout position.
The number of worked-example preference questions shown in the top panel.
The layer of the top panel's readouts, roughly three quarters of the way through the model's depth, within the workspace band where lens readouts are most interpretable.
The layer range averaged over in the bottom panel's mass metrics; approximately the paper's workspace band, avoiding the noisy sensory layers and the output-tied motor layers.
The number of prefill conditions compared in the bottom panel: preferred option, dispreferred option, third-person incorrect preference, factual error.
On dispreferred-option prefills, the fraction of cases where the model goes on to argue for the prefilled option - the behavioral evidence that the conflict signal is never voiced.
On dispreferred-option prefills, the fraction of cases where the model simply emits an end-of-turn token instead of continuing.
The single remaining dispreferred-option trial, in which the model backtracks only to say it has no preferences - still not arguing for the preferred option.

On the factual-error and third-person controls, the fraction of cases where the model argues for the prefilled incorrect option; in nearly every other case it corrects itself or ends the turn. The contrast with 88% shows the model treats violations of its own preferences differently in behavior, yet objects only internally.
